on an eight-core machine and change nothing else? Take 10 minutes.

runs a single-threaded executor: one thread takes one ready callback at a time, and while that thread is inside the service callback it takes nothing else. For those 2 seconds the node runs no timer, no subscription callback and no second service request.

In the second after the service returns, the timer runs 20 times, not 60. rcl does not queue the periods that passed. When a timer is overdue it moves the next call time forward by whole periods and calls the callback once (
). Missed ticks are lost, not owed.

Nothing changes with the multi-threaded executor. Every entity created without a callback group belongs to the node's default group, and that group is mutually exclusive, so no two of its callbacks run at the same time. Eight threads that are all forbidden to take a second callback out of the same group behave like one. The Jazzy guide on callback groups puts it the same way: a node whose entities all share one mutually exclusive group acts as if a single-threaded executor were running it.

You pass if all three answers are right. Getting the first two and missing the third is a partial pass, and it is the usual gap: the executor decides how many threads exist, the callback groups decide what those threads are allowed to do. Answering that the timer queues its missed ticks is a fail, because it leads to code that measures time by counting its own callbacks.
An executor decides which thread runs a node's callbacks: it watches a wait set of timers, subscriptions, services and clients, and hands one ready one at a time to a thread.
is the simplest case: one thread takes one ready callback, runs it, and asks again. A

decides what may run at once: a mutually exclusive group never runs two of its own callbacks together, a reentrant group lets its callbacks overlap themselves and each other, and callbacks in two different groups may always run together, whatever kind either is. Anything created without naming a group lands in the node's default, mutually exclusive group.

The problem this solves is letting some callbacks run at once without a lock on every piece of shared state. A control loop's timer and the odometry it reads can share one mutually exclusive group, so the executor guarantees they never run together and their shared state needs no mutex; a slow, occasional service can sit in a group of its own so it never holds up that timer.

A mutually exclusive group is a lock built into the executor: only one thread may run a callback from it at a time, on any number of threads. A multi-threaded executor changes anything only once work is split across groups. Anything crossing a group boundary, a value one group's callback writes and another's reads, is a data race once two groups can run at once, needing its own protection, an atomic being the cheapest one.

The mistake under pressure is waiting for a service's answer inside a callback sharing a mutually exclusive group with the client: the answer arrives only when a thread runs the client's callback, and every thread is forbidden from taking a second callback out of that group while the first waits, so adding threads changes nothing. A quieter version hits timers: an overdue one skips the ticks it missed and fires once, so code counting its own timer calls to measure elapsed time is wrong exactly when the node is busiest.

You meet exactly this in the interview question itself: a controller on a 20 Hz timer and a service whose callback takes two seconds, both in the node's default group, where the timer stops for those two seconds under
, and stays stopped the same way after swapping in a multi-threaded executor with nothing else changed.

"Ask for the next ready piece of work" is where the design lives. The executor builds a

out of the node's timers, subscriptions, services, clients and waitables, hands it to rcl and blocks. The middleware wakes it when something is ready. What comes back is one flag per entity: this subscription has at least one message, that timer is due. Not how many messages, and not when they arrived. Messages stay in the middleware's own queue until a callback takes one, which is why the depth in the QoS profile is the queue that matters and the executor is the only thing that drains it. The Jazzy documentation calls that a deliberate difference from ROS 1, where the client library kept its own queue.

One flag per entity has a consequence people meet as a bug. The executor cannot serve messages in arrival order, because it does not know the arrival order. It walks the ready entities and takes one message from each, then waits again. The Jazzy documentation calls this round robin rather than first in, first out, and Casini and colleagues described it in their 2019 paper on ROS 2 response times. Here is the shape of it, with the middleware queues and one pass of the wait set modelled in plain C++. A callback has held the only thread for 2 seconds, odometry arrives 50 times a second into a queue of depth 10, and scans arrive 10 times a second into a queue of depth 5:

blocks.text:
odom: 100 delivered, 90 dropped, 10 waiting
scan: 20 delivered, 15 dropped, 5 waiting
three passes over the wait set: odom 91, scan 16, odom 92, scan 17, odom 93, scan 18

c.v: Two things to take from the numbers. A 2-second callback costs 90 odometry messages and 15 scans, and no error is raised anywhere: the queue drops the oldest to make room, exactly as

asked it to. And when the thread comes back, the first odometry message it sees is number 91, which arrived at 1.82 seconds and is 0.18 seconds old. The node is a fifth of a second behind rather than one message behind, because the queue is holding ten messages and the oldest of them is the one it has to handle first, and the 90 that were dropped never come back.

Threads alone give you nothing, because a
decides what may overlap. There are two kinds, and rclcpp's

states the contract of each. Callbacks in a mutually exclusive group are never run more than once at a time, and never at the same time as another callback of the same group. Callbacks in a reentrant group may run at the same time as themselves and as each other. Callbacks in different groups may always run at the same time, whatever the type of either group.
Read that last sentence twice, because it is the one that surprises people. Two mutually exclusive groups do not exclude each other. Mutual exclusion holds inside a group, never between groups.

Every node has a default callback group, and it is mutually exclusive. Anything you create without naming a group lands there, which is what makes an unmodified node safe under any executor and also what makes a multi-threaded executor pointless until you split something out. You make a group with
, and you pass it as the last argument of
. Keep the group in a member: as with subscriptions, a group you do not hold is dropped, and the executor stops triggering its callbacks.

Two further properties are worth knowing. An entity passes its group on to every callback it creates, so an action client in a group hands that group to its goal, feedback and result callbacks. And a group's mutual exclusion is one atomic flag,

, that a thread clears while it holds work from the group; when the work is done, the multi-threaded executor triggers a guard condition so a waiting thread rebuilds its wait set and can take the group's next callback.

That flag is also the whole deadlock. If a callback in group G waits for a result that only another callback in group G can deliver, no thread is allowed to deliver it, and both wait forever. A service response is the common case:

returns a future that becomes ready when the executor hands the response to the client, and if the client and the caller share one mutually exclusive group, the caller is holding the one permission needed to do that. The services topic showed the same hang under
; the exercise below shows that a multi-threaded executor does not fix it on its own, and which change does.
Timers belong in this picture too.

A control timer in a mutually exclusive group cannot overlap itself, which is what you want for a loop that publishes commands: a second copy of the control step running in parallel with the first would compute a command from half-updated state. A timer in a reentrant group can overlap itself, and then it can hand a long tick and a short tick to two threads at once.

None of this changes what your code computes. The executor decides when a callback runs and on which thread; it never decides what the callback works out. So the rule from the earlier topics holds, and gets sharper here: keep the node's logic in plain classes with no ROS types and no clock, take the time and the inputs as arguments, and leave the callback with the translation. Run b fails because the number of threads was never the constraint.

puts the client and the timer in one mutually exclusive group, and that group's rule is that no two of its callbacks run at the same time. The response arrives as a callback of the client, which is in the group; the timer callback holds the group. Seven idle threads change nothing, because none of them is allowed to take the response. The Jazzy guide on callback groups states the exact condition: the timer and the client must not be in the same mutually exclusive group.

While run a's node is stuck, it receives nothing else either. Every subscription, every other service and the parameter services of that node are in its default callback group and behind the same one thread, and their messages pile up in the middleware until their queues drop the oldest. 5 seconds of a 50 Hz input at depth 10 is 250 messages arriving and 240 dropped.
Two more things the runs teach.
